title: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait
sections: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy (Q1-Q50)

questions.text: Which of the following best describes the stance phase of the gait cycle?
options: The period when the foot is completely off the ground
The period when the foot is in contact with the ground
The period when both feet are off the ground
The period between heel-off and toe-off only
questions.correctAnswer: B. The period when the foot is in contact with the ground
questions.explanation: The stance phase occurs while the foot is in contact with the ground and occupies about 60% of normal walking.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT one of the principal arches of the foot?
questions.explanation: The principal arches are the medial longitudinal, lateral longitudinal and transverse arches.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: During normal walking, which muscle controls the lowering of the forefoot immediately after heel contact?
questions.explanation: Tibialis anterior contracts eccentrically after initial contact to control the lowering of the forefoot.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: Which bone is the keystone of the medial longitudinal arch?
questions.explanation: The head of the talus is the keystone of the medial longitudinal arch.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: Injury to the common fibular nerve may produce foot drop. Which gait abnormality may compensate for this?
questions.explanation: A high-stepping gait helps clear the toes when ankle dorsiflexion is weak.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: Which ligament is particularly important in supporting the head of the talus and maintaining the medial longitudinal arch?
questions.explanation: The plantar calcaneonavicular ligament supports the talar head and is also called the spring ligament.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: Which muscle group provides a major propulsive force during terminal stance?
questions.explanation: The gastrocnemius and soleus contribute to propulsion during late stance and push-off.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: Which muscle provides important dynamic support to the medial longitudinal arch?
questions.explanation: Tibialis posterior is a major dynamic support of the medial longitudinal arch.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: During the swing phase, which ankle movement helps prevent the toes from dragging?
questions.explanation: Dorsiflexion keeps the toes clear of the ground during swing.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: Which structure is a major passive support of the longitudinal arches?
questions.explanation: The plantar aponeurosis resists separation of the ends of the arches.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: A Trendelenburg gait most commonly indicates weakness of which muscle group?
questions.explanation: Weak hip abductors allow the pelvis to drop on the unsupported side during single-limb support.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: Which bones form the principal framework of the lateral longitudinal arch?
options: Calcaneus, cuboid and fourth and fifth metatarsals
questions.correctAnswer: B. Calcaneus, cuboid and fourth and fifth metatarsals
questions.explanation: The lateral longitudinal arch is formed mainly by the calcaneus, cuboid and lateral metatarsals.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: Which nerve supplies gluteus medius and gluteus minimus?
questions.explanation: The superior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus medius and minimus, as well as tensor fasciae latae.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: The plantar calcaneonavicular ligament is commonly known as the:
questions.explanation: The spring ligament supports the head of the talus.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: When both feet are simultaneously in contact with the ground during walking, the period is called:
questions.explanation: Double support occurs when both feet contact the ground at the same time.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: Which muscle is particularly associated with supporting the transverse arch of the foot?
questions.explanation: Fibularis longus crosses the sole and helps support the transverse arch.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: Which muscle helps stabilise the pelvis during single-limb support?
questions.explanation: Gluteus medius helps prevent excessive pelvic drop on the unsupported side.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: A markedly lowered medial longitudinal arch is called:
questions.explanation: Pes planus means a low or flattened medial longitudinal arch.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: Which gait pattern may occur when a person reduces the time spent bearing weight on a painful limb?
questions.explanation: An antalgic gait reduces stance time on the painful side.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: The tendon of fibularis longus inserts into the:
options: Base of the fifth metatarsal only
Base of the first metatarsal and medial cuneiform
questions.correctAnswer: B. Base of the first metatarsal and medial cuneiform
questions.explanation: Fibularis longus crosses the sole to insert on the first metatarsal base and medial cuneiform.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: Which phase of gait involves acceptance of body weight after initial contact?
questions.explanation: During loading response, the limb accepts body weight and absorbs shock.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: Which ligament is a major passive support of the lateral longitudinal arch?
questions.explanation: The long plantar ligament supports the lateral longitudinal arch and the calcaneocuboid region.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: Which muscle group is important for preventing the knee from buckling during loading response?
questions.explanation: The quadriceps control knee flexion as body weight is accepted.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: The transverse arch is formed primarily by the:
options: Cuneiforms, cuboid and bases of the metatarsals
questions.correctAnswer: C. Cuneiforms, cuboid and bases of the metatarsals
questions.explanation: The transverse arch involves the cuneiforms, cuboid and metatarsal bases.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: Which muscle is most important in controlling forward progression of the tibia over the foot during midstance?
questions.explanation: The soleus and other plantar flexors control forward tibial progression during stance.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: Which of the following best describes the function of the foot arches?
options: Distribute body weight and absorb shock
questions.correctAnswer: B. Distribute body weight and absorb shock
questions.explanation: The arches distribute weight, absorb shock and provide both flexibility and stability.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: Which nerve supplies the principal ankle plantar flexors?
questions.explanation: The tibial nerve supplies gastrocnemius, soleus and other major plantar flexors.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: Toe extension tightens the plantar aponeurosis and raises the longitudinal arch. This is called the:
questions.explanation: The windlass mechanism tensions the plantar aponeurosis during toe extension.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: The swing phase occupies approximately what percentage of normal walking?
questions.explanation: The swing phase occupies about 40% of the gait cycle.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: Which muscle is supplied by the medial plantar nerve and contributes to dynamic support of the medial arch?
questions.explanation: Abductor hallucis is supplied by the medial plantar nerve and supports the medial side of the foot.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: Which muscle helps control the trunk and hip during early stance?
questions.explanation: Gluteus maximus helps provide hip extension stability during early stance.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: Which bone is generally considered the keystone of the lateral longitudinal arch?
questions.explanation: The cuboid is commonly described as the keystone of the lateral longitudinal arch.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: Which muscle assists hip flexion during early swing?
questions.explanation: Iliopsoas is an important hip flexor during limb advancement.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: Which statement about the medial and lateral longitudinal arches is correct?
options: The medial arch is lower and less mobile
The lateral arch is relatively low and provides a stable platform
The transverse arch is formed only by the phalanges
questions.correctAnswer: C. The lateral arch is relatively low and provides a stable platform
questions.explanation: The lateral longitudinal arch is relatively low and rigid, providing a stable weight-bearing platform.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: During terminal swing, the hamstrings mainly:
options: Decelerate forward movement of the thigh and leg
questions.correctAnswer: B. Decelerate forward movement of the thigh and leg
questions.explanation: The hamstrings eccentrically decelerate the limb before initial contact.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: Which of the following is a major bony component of the medial longitudinal arch?
questions.explanation: The talus is a key component and the keystone of the medial longitudinal arch.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: Which joint movement contributes directly to propulsion during push-off?
options: Movement at the distal tibiofibular joint
questions.explanation: Ankle plantar flexion contributes to forward propulsion in late stance.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: Weakness of which muscle may cause a backward trunk lean to compensate for reduced hip extension stability?
questions.explanation: Gluteus maximus weakness may produce a gluteus maximus lurch.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: Which of the following best describes the windlass mechanism?
options: Toe extension tensions the plantar aponeurosis and elevates the arch
Ankle inversion relaxes all foot ligaments
Knee extension raises the transverse arch directly
Toe flexion removes tension from the plantar aponeurosis
questions.correctAnswer: A. Toe extension tensions the plantar aponeurosis and elevates the arch
questions.explanation: Extension of the metatarsophalangeal joints winds the plantar aponeurosis around the metatarsal heads.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: Which statement about the medial longitudinal arch is correct?
options: It is higher and more flexible than the lateral arch
It is lower and more rigid than the lateral arch
It is supported only by bone
questions.correctAnswer: A. It is higher and more flexible than the lateral arch
questions.explanation: The medial longitudinal arch is higher and more elastic than the lateral arch.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: Which gait abnormality is associated with weakness of ankle dorsiflexors?
options: Foot drop with possible high-stepping gait
questions.correctAnswer: A. Foot drop with possible high-stepping gait
questions.explanation: Dorsiflexor weakness may cause foot drop and compensatory high stepping.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: Which structure connects the calcaneus to the navicular and supports the talar head?
questions.explanation: The spring ligament extends from the calcaneus to the navicular and supports the head of the talus.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: Which of the following is the correct sequence of gait phases?
options: Initial contact → loading response → midstance → terminal stance → pre-swing → initial swing → midswing → terminal swing
Initial swing → loading response → terminal stance → midstance → terminal swing
Loading response → initial contact → midswing → terminal stance → pre-swing
Initial contact → terminal swing → midstance → loading response → initial swing
questions.correctAnswer: A. Initial contact → loading response → midstance → terminal stance → pre-swing → initial swing → midswing → terminal swing
questions.explanation: This is the recognised sequence of the eight gait-cycle phases.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: Which combination correctly identifies important supports of the medial longitudinal arch?
options: Spring ligament, plantar aponeurosis and tibialis posterior
Patellar ligament, iliotibial tract and sartorius
Anterior talofibular ligament, biceps femoris and popliteus
Deltoid ligament, quadriceps femoris and gracilis
questions.correctAnswer: A. Spring ligament, plantar aponeurosis and tibialis posterior
questions.explanation: The spring ligament and plantar aponeurosis provide passive support, while tibialis posterior provides dynamic support.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: What is a major role of the arms during normal walking?
options: They help balance and counterbalance trunk and lower-limb movements
They generate the primary propulsive force
questions.correctAnswer: B. They help balance and counterbalance trunk and lower-limb movements
questions.explanation: Arm swing helps balance and counterbalances trunk and pelvic rotation.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: Which of the following best describes pre-swing?
options: The limb accepts initial body weight
The body moves over the supporting foot only
Weight transfers to the opposite limb as the toes prepare to leave the ground
The limb advances forward without ground contact
questions.correctAnswer: C. Weight transfers to the opposite limb as the toes prepare to leave the ground
questions.explanation: Pre-swing is the final part of stance, when weight is transferred and the limb prepares for toe-off.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: Which ligament helps maintain the lateral longitudinal arch by supporting the calcaneocuboid region?
questions.explanation: The long plantar ligament is a key passive support of the lateral longitudinal arch.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: Which muscle controls plantar flexion of the foot immediately after initial contact?
questions.explanation: Tibialis anterior contracts eccentrically to control the foot as the forefoot lowers.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: Weakness of tibialis posterior can compromise which structure most directly?
questions.explanation: Tibialis posterior is a major dynamic support of the medial longitudinal arch.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy

questions.text: Which gait phase occurs immediately before initial contact of the same limb?
questions.explanation: Terminal swing is the final swing phase before the foot makes initial contact.
questions.section: Arches of the Foot & Walking Gait: Biomechanics & Functional Anatomy
